sections.title: Wiring methods — general rules
sections.plain_explanation: Article 300 is the rulebook that sits over every wiring method in this chapter. Whichever cable or raceway you pick later — NM, MC, EMT, PVC — these general rules still apply: protect the wiring from damage, give underground runs enough cover, support what you install, and leave enough free wire at every box to make a proper joint. Read this article first, then go to the article for the specific method.
sections.on_the_job: Before you choose a method, ask three questions: Where does it run (dry, damp, wet, underground, exposed)? What can hit it? How will it be supported? The answers pick the method and trigger the 300 rules.
sections.figure_idea: Cross-section of a house wall, slab and yard showing one circuit as NM in the wall, EMT on the surface and UF underground, with callouts to 300.4, 300.5 and 300.11.

sections.title: All conductors of a circuit run together
sections.plain_explanation: Every conductor of a circuit — the ungrounded conductors, the grounded (neutral) conductor, and the equipment grounding conductor — is installed in the same raceway, cable, trench, or cord. The rule keeps the circuit's magnetic fields canceling each other (conductors run separately heat surrounding metal and behave unpredictably), and it guarantees the ground path travels with the circuit it protects. The exceptions are narrow — conductors in parallel sets, and a few underground and existing-installation arrangements this section names — and even they require the conductors to be grouped so each raceway or cable carries a complete, balanced set.
sections.on_the_job: The field failure is the borrowed ground or the lone neutral: a ground pulled from a different cable, or one circuit's neutral run in another conduit. If the conductors did not arrive together, they do not splice together — re-pull the run.
sections.figure_idea: One conduit with hot, neutral, and ground entering together (correct), and a second conduit carrying only a stray ground borrowed from another run (crossed out).

sections.title: Protecting wiring from physical damage
sections.plain_explanation: This is the nail-and-screw section. Where cable or raceway passes through or runs alongside wood or metal framing, it has to sit far enough back from the face of the framing that drywall screws and nails miss it — or be shielded by a steel plate. It also covers cables run across the top of joists, through notches, and parallel to framing, where the same idea applies: keep the wiring out of the fastener zone, or armor it.
sections.on_the_job: Center your holes, keep the 1-1/4 in setback in 300.4(A)(1), and plate anything that ends up closer. Kick plates / nail plates are not extras — if the cable is in the strike zone, the plate goes on before drywall, every time.
sections.sharma_note: Kick plates are always in Sharma takeoffs — stock them on every rough-in truck, do not treat them as an optional add-on.
sections.figure_idea: Front view of a stud bay: a centered bored hole marked 1-1/4 in minimum from each face, and beside it a shallow hole covered by a 1/16 in steel nail plate.

sections.title: Bored holes in wood framing
sections.plain_explanation: A hole bored through a wood stud or joist for cable or raceway must be drilled so the edge of the hole is at least 1-1/4 in from the nearest edge of the wood. If that distance cannot be kept, the cable must be protected by a steel plate at least 1/16 in thick, of a suitable length and width, installed to protect the wiring.
sections.on_the_job: Drill in the middle third of the stud width where you can. Check both faces — a hole can be legal from the front and too close from the back on a shallow stud. Plate first, then pull cable, so the plate is not forgotten.
sections.figure_idea: Close-up of a 2x4 stud with a centered hole, dimension arrows showing 1-1/4 in from hole edge to stud face.

sections.title: Cables through metal framing — bushings and plates
sections.plain_explanation: Metal studs change the protection hardware. Where a cable passes through a hole in a metal framing member, it is protected by a bushing or a listed grommet that covers the sharp edge of the hole and is designed to stay in place. Where a cable runs in a slot or notch in metal framing, it is protected against nails and screws by a steel plate at least 1/16 in thick, or by a bushing or grommet listed for the purpose. A raw punched steel edge will saw through a cable jacket under vibration and thermal movement — the bushing is not optional trim.
sections.on_the_job: Stock grommets on the truck for steel-stud work and snap them in as you lay out the holes, not after the cable is pulled — a grommet forced over a pulled cable usually ends up in a pocket instead. Walk the run before insulation: every hole, every cable, one bushing.
sections.figure_idea: Steel stud with three holes: a bare punched hole with cable through it (crossed out), a hole with a snap-in grommet, and a slotted run protected by a 1/16 in plate.

sections.title: Cables and raceways parallel to framing members and furring strips
sections.plain_explanation: This is the along-the-framing companion to the bored-hole rule. In exposed or concealed work, where a cable or raceway runs parallel to a framing member — a joist, rafter or stud — or parallel to furring strips, it has to be installed and supported so the nearest outside surface of the cable or raceway is at least 1-1/4 in from the nearest edge of the framing member or furring strip, wherever nails or screws are likely to penetrate. Where that distance cannot be kept, the cable or raceway must be protected from nail or screw penetration by a steel plate, sleeve or equivalent at least 1/16 in thick; a listed and marked thinner steel plate that provides equal or better protection is also permitted. Steel plates are not required for rigid metal conduit, IMC, rigid nonmetallic conduit or EMT — the raceway is its own protection — and for concealed work in finished buildings, cables may be fished between access points where supporting them is impracticable.
sections.on_the_job: Running down a stud bay or along a joist, keep the cable centered or held 1-1/4 in off the edge the drywall screws will come through — cable stackers and standoffs exist for exactly this. If a stretch of the run has to hug the edge, plate that stretch before the wall closes.
sections.figure_idea: Side view of a stud bay: a cable running vertically along a stud, held 1-1/4 in from the stud's nearest edge by a cable stacker, with a second run tight to the edge covered by a 1/16 in steel plate.

sections.title: Protecting large conductors where they enter enclosures
sections.plain_explanation: Conductors 4 AWG and larger entering a cabinet, box or raceway have to be protected from abrasion at the entry — by a fitting, bushing or adapter that gives them a smooth, rounded surface to bear on, in the cases this subsection describes. Big conductors are stiff, heavy and expensive; a sharp knockout edge plus one hard pull is insulation damage you cannot see after the cover goes on. The research notes this protection was expanded and clarified for 2020; the exact fitting language is Mike's to confirm.
sections.on_the_job: Fit the insulating bushing before the pull, not after you see the scrape. On service and feeder entries, check every entry edge with a fingertip before conductors go in.
sections.figure_idea: Service conductor entering a meter enclosure through a listed fitting with a smooth rounded insulating surface, sharp-edge version crossed out beside it.

sections.title: Underground wiring — cover, protection and sealing
sections.plain_explanation: Underground runs have to be in a wiring method approved for burial and buried deep enough that digging, traffic and frost do not reach them. Cover is measured from the top of the cable or raceway to finished grade, and the required depth depends on the method and what is above it — a yard, a driveway and a slab are not the same row of the table. Risers coming out of the ground need protection from damage. Under 300.5(G), a raceway through which moisture could contact energized live parts has to be sealed or plugged at either or both ends, with a sealant identified for use with the cable or conductor insulation; the separate seal for a raceway that passes between different temperatures, where condensation is known to be a problem, is in 300.7(A), not in this section. Direct-buried splices and taps are permitted without a splice box only when made under 110.14(B), and wire connectors or splicing means used for direct burial must be listed for that use.
sections.on_the_job: The rows Sharma digs to most (Table 300.5, cover over the top of the cable or raceway): in open ground — direct-burial cable 24 in, nonmetallic raceway (PVC) 18 in, rigid metal conduit 6 in. Under a one- or two-family dwelling driveway or outdoor parking area used only for the dwelling — direct-burial cable, rigid metal conduit, and nonmetallic raceway (PVC) are all 18 in. The 12 in figure is only the separate column for a 120 V, 20 A or less, GFCI-protected residential branch circuit. It is not the depth for PVC in general. Under streets, roads, alleys, driveways and parking lots (the commercial row) — 24 in for EVERY method. A residential branch circuit 120V, 20A or less with GFCI protection gets the 12 in column in its own row. Slabs and building interiors have their own rows — check the table row for the actual location before you trench, and never carry one depth to every location.
sections.figure_idea: Trench cross-section with four parallel runs at 24, 18, 12 and 6 in, each labeled with its method, and a tape measure to finished grade.
sections.florida_note: NEC 300.5(D)(3) itself requires a warning ribbon — that part is code, not local preference — but only for underground service conductors that are not encased in concrete and are buried 18 in or more below grade: their location must be identified by a warning ribbon placed in the trench at least 12 in above the underground installation. The NEC does not impose that ribbon rule on ordinary feeders and branch circuits. Local AHJs may add bedding or tape requirements beyond it — confirm at permit, and do not assume the table is the whole job.

sections.title: Sealing raceways that pass between different temperatures
sections.plain_explanation: Where part of a raceway sits at a much lower temperature than another part — a run from a warm building into a cold-storage room is the textbook case — the warmer air inside the raceway circulates into the cold part and its moisture condenses there, wetting conductors that were installed dry. This section requires the raceway to be filled with an approved sealing material at the temperature boundary, to stop that air circulation. It is a condensation seal, not a waterproofing seal: the separate rule for sealing a raceway so moisture cannot reach live parts is 300.5(G), and explosionproof sealing fittings are a hazardous-location subject in Article 501, not this section.
sections.on_the_job: The Florida case is any conduit that leaves a hot attic or a sun-baked exterior wall and enters an air-conditioned space or a walk-in cooler: put the duct seal in the run where the temperature changes, on the warm side of the boundary, before the conductors are pulled or as the section's method directs. A run that drips at the panel in August is usually this rule, missed.
sections.figure_idea: A conduit crossing a wall from a sunlit exterior into a cooler interior, with a seal drawn inside the conduit at the wall line and condensation drops shown on the unsealed version beside it.

sections.title: Securing and supporting — general
sections.plain_explanation: Wiring methods must be secured in place and supported at the intervals their own article requires. Raceways and cables cannot hang off other raceways, pipes or ceiling wires unless the rule for that method specifically allows it, and in a fire-rated ceiling the support has to be independent so the wiring does not fall when the ceiling does.
sections.on_the_job: When in doubt, support it yourself: your own strap, on structure, at the spacing in the method's article (334.30 for NM, 330.30 for MC, 358.30 for EMT, 352.30 for PVC). Never lay cable on a ceiling tile or tie it to a sprinkler pipe.

sections.title: Free conductor length at boxes
sections.plain_explanation: At every outlet, junction and switch point, leave at least 6 in of free conductor, measured from where the conductor comes out of its raceway or cable sheath. Where the box opening is smaller than 8 in in any direction, the conductors also have to stick out of the opening by at least 3 in, so devices can be made up and folded back without fighting short wires. Conductors that pass straight through a box without a splice or termination are not counted by this rule.
sections.on_the_job: Strip and make up with the full 6 in in hand. If you are short, the fix is a bigger pull or a re-pull — not a wire nut buried with 2 in stubs. Leave the same working length on the spare conductors you cap off.
sections.figure_idea: Side view of a single-gang box with 6 in of conductor looped out, and a 3 in dimension from the box opening.

sections.title: A box or fitting at each splice, outlet and junction
sections.plain_explanation: Where the wiring method is conduit, tubing, Type AC cable, Type MC cable, Type MI cable, nonmetallic-sheathed cable or another cable method, a box or conduit body has to be installed at each conductor splice point, outlet point, switch point, junction point, termination point and pull point — unless one of the exceptions in 300.15(A) through (L) permits otherwise for that case. A fitting identified for the use may be used in place of a box or conduit body where conductors are not spliced or terminated inside the fitting, and that fitting has to stay accessible after installation unless it is listed for concealed installation. Boxes themselves have to stay accessible under 314.29, without tearing the building apart. A joint made in open air, in a wall cavity, or inside a raceway run, with no exception behind it, is not a joint the next electrician — or an inspector — can ever find.
sections.on_the_job: Plan box locations while the walls are open. If a splice has to exist, it gets a box with a cover that stays reachable after finishes go on.

sections.title: Finish the raceway before the wire goes in
sections.plain_explanation: A raceway system is installed complete — runs finished, boxes set, fittings in place — before the conductors are pulled into it. Cut ends are reamed or otherwise finished so no sharp edge waits inside to skin insulation during the pull. Short sections are the everyday case, not a loophole: a nipple between two enclosures follows its own fill rules, but it is still a finished piece of raceway before wire enters it. Pulling wire into a half-built run and 'finishing around it' damages insulation where nobody can see it.
sections.on_the_job: Walk the run with a flashlight before the pull: every coupling tight, every end reamed, bushings on. The time to find a burr is before 200 ft of THHN is sitting in the pipe.
sections.figure_idea: Conduit run in two states: complete with reamed ends and bushings, wire spool staged (ready); versus a gap in the run with wire already threaded through it (crossed out).

sections.title: Firestopping penetrations of rated construction
sections.plain_explanation: Where wiring passes through a fire-rated floor, wall or ceiling, the opening around it has to be firestopped with an approved system so fire and smoke do not travel through the penetration. The electrical work does not end at the conduit — the annular space around it is part of the rated assembly's performance. Ordinary expanding foam from the truck is not a firestop system unless it is listed as one for that assembly and penetration.
sections.on_the_job: On commercial and multi-family work, plan the firestop with the run: listed system for the assembly, the raceway type and the opening size, installed before the wall is signed off. Photograph it — the next inspector cannot see inside a closed wall either.
sections.figure_idea: Rated wall section with a conduit penetration sealed by a red listed firestop system, callout 'system matched to assembly — not generic foam'.
sections.florida_note: Firestop systems are assembly-specific; Florida inspectors on rated multi-family and commercial work check them by listing, not by color.

sections.title: Wiring in ducts, plenums and other air-handling spaces
sections.plain_explanation: Spaces made for moving environmental air — ducts, plenums and the space above a ceiling used as a return-air plenum — restrict what wiring may run there and how, because anything burning or smoldering in that space feeds the whole building's air. Only the wiring methods and materials this section allows may be installed, and equipment in those spaces is limited to what the section and the mechanical rules permit.
sections.on_the_job: The field trap is the plenum ceiling that looks like an ordinary ceiling: before you run a method through a ceiling space on commercial work, ask whether that space is a return-air plenum. If it is, the method list shrinks — when in doubt, ask the AHJ before rough-in, not at inspection.
sections.figure_idea: Reflected ceiling plan with the return-air plenum shaded and two wiring methods shown: one allowed routing tagged, one barred routing crossed out.

sections.title: Wiring in exit enclosures
sections.plain_explanation: Exit enclosures — the protected stair towers and exit passageways people escape through — may contain only the wiring that serves the exit enclosure itself and the limited other wiring this section permits. Ordinary branch circuits passing through a stair tower on their way somewhere else do not belong there. This section was new in the 2020 NEC, which is why older study material and older habits do not mention it.
sections.on_the_job: On multi-family and commercial work, route around the stair tower by default. If a run must enter it, stop and check what it serves before it goes in.
sections.figure_idea: Building section of a stair tower with a foreign branch circuit shown re-routed around the enclosure and only the tower's own lighting circuit inside.

sections.title: Conductors for general wiring
sections.plain_explanation: Article 310 is about the conductors themselves: what they are made of, how they are insulated, and — most used of all — how much current they may carry. The ampacity work lives in 310.12 for dwelling services and feeders, 310.15 for correction and adjustment, and Table 310.16 for the ampacity values themselves. Termination temperature limits live back in 110.14(C) in Chapter 1; this article hands you the number, Chapter 1 tells you which column you may actually use.
sections.on_the_job: Start every sizing question here in this order: load, then Table 310.16 column allowed by the terminations, then correction/adjustment in 310.15, then the small-conductor caps in 240.4(D) from Chapter 2.
sections.figure_idea: Flowchart with four boxes: Load -> Table 310.16 -> 310.15 correction/adjustment -> 240.4(D) cap.

sections.title: Conductor minimums — size, material, stranding
sections.plain_explanation: This section sets the floor for building wire. The smallest conductor for branch circuits and feeders is 14 AWG copper or 12 AWG aluminum or copper-clad aluminum — which is why there is no 14 AWG CCA branch-circuit wire in 2020 work. Conductors are copper, aluminum, or copper-clad aluminum, and the material decides which ampacity column and which termination rules apply. Conductors 8 AWG and larger installed in raceways are stranded. Smaller conductors and special circuits (fixture wires, control and signaling circuits, and the other cases other articles govern) follow their own articles — this floor is for general wiring.
sections.on_the_job: Ordering rule that follows from this page: a '14 AWG' line on a takeoff means copper. If the job is CCA, the smallest branch-circuit reel on the truck is 12 AWG — and per S-10 it lands on a 15A breaker, not a 20A.
sections.sharma_note: S-10: copper by default; CCA one size up. This section is where the 'no 14 AWG CCA' rule lives.
sections.figure_idea: Three reels labeled by material with their minimum branch-circuit sizes: copper 14 AWG, aluminum 12 AWG, CCA 12 AWG.

sections.title: The dwelling 83% rule for services and whole-load feeders
sections.plain_explanation:
For a single-phase dwelling service rated 100A through 400A that carries the entire load of the house, the service conductors may be sized at 83% of the service rating instead of the full Table 310.16 ampacity. The same idea applies to a feeder that carries the entire dwelling load, such as the feeder from an outside meter-main to the inside main panel. It does not apply to a partial-load feeder, and it does not apply when temperature correction or bundling adjustment is in play.

Table 310.12 in full — the service or whole-load feeder rating, then the conductor it permits:
• 100A — 4 AWG copper / 2 AWG aluminum
• 110A — 3 AWG copper / 1 AWG aluminum
• 125A — 2 AWG copper / 1/0 aluminum
• 150A — 1 AWG copper / 2/0 aluminum
• 175A — 1/0 copper / 3/0 aluminum
• 200A — 2/0 copper / 4/0 aluminum
• 225A — 3/0 copper / 250 kcmil aluminum
• 250A — 4/0 copper / 300 kcmil aluminum
• 300A — 250 kcmil copper / 350 kcmil aluminum
• 350A — 350 kcmil copper / 500 kcmil aluminum
• 400A — 400 kcmil copper / 600 kcmil aluminum
sections.on_the_job: The pair Sharma uses daily: a 200A house service is 2/0 copper or 4/0 aluminum when this rule applies. A feeder to a garage subpanel that carries only part of the house load gets sized at full value from Table 310.16 — no 83%.
sections.figure_idea: One-line of a house: meter-main outside, main panel inside, the feeder between them labeled 'whole load — 83% can apply'; a second feeder to a garage labeled 'partial load — full size'.

sections.title: Ampacity correction (temperature) and adjustment (bundling)
sections.plain_explanation:
Table 310.16 assumes no more than three current-carrying conductors together and a 30°C (86°F) surrounding temperature. When reality is hotter, or more conductors share a raceway or cable, the ampacity goes down: an ambient correction factor for temperature, and an adjustment factor for the count of current-carrying conductors — 80% for 4 to 6, 70% for 7 to 9, 50% for 10 to 20, 45% for 21 to 30, 40% for 31 to 40, and 35% for 41 or more. Equipment grounding conductors do not count, and a neutral that carries only the unbalanced load of its circuit usually does not count either. You may start the math from the conductor's insulation rating (for example the 90°C column for THHN or NM conductors) as long as the final number does not exceed what the termination column and the method's own limit allow.

The ambient correction factors themselves (Table 310.15(B)(1)), for the temperature bands above the 30°C base:
• At 36–40°C — 0.82 for a 60°C conductor, 0.88 for 75°C, 0.91 for 90°C
• At 41–45°C — 0.71 / 0.82 / 0.87
• At 46–50°C — 0.58 / 0.75 / 0.82
• At 51–55°C — 0.41 / 0.67 / 0.76
• At 56–60°C — the 60°C column no longer corrects (shown as — in the table) / 0.58 / 0.71
• At 61–70°C — — / 0.33 / 0.58
Where both apply, the two factors multiply: a bundled run in a hot attic takes the count factor and the temperature factor together.
sections.on_the_job:
Count current-carrying conductors honestly on a home-run bundle: three 12/2 NM cables bundled over 24 in is six current-carrying conductors, not three circuits at full ampacity. Hot Florida attics are the ambient case Sharma hits most — see the attic tip AH-07, whose 310.15(B)(1) citation Mike should re-check against the 2020 numbering.

Worked example: 12 AWG THHN starts at 30A in the 90°C column. In a 50°C attic the correction is 0.82, giving 24.6A — still enough for its 20A breaker. Run as NM cable, the same conductor is capped at its 60°C table value of 20A before the 240.4(D) cap is even reached, so a single attic circuit rarely changes; a bundle of home runs, where the count factor stacks on the temperature factor, is where the answer moves.
sections.figure_idea: Bar chart: one raceway at 3, 6 and 9 current-carrying conductors with the 100%, 80% and 70% factors marked.
sections.florida_note: Florida attics routinely run far above 30°C in summer; that is a design condition here, not an edge case.

sections.title: Table 310.16 — how to read the ampacity table
sections.plain_explanation:
Table 310.16 gives the allowable ampacity of an insulated conductor by size, material and temperature column: 60°C, 75°C and 90°C, for copper on the left and for aluminum and copper-clad aluminum together on the right. Read it in four steps. One, find the size. Two, pick the material column — CCA is read in the aluminum columns, never the copper columns. Three, pick the temperature column your terminations allow under 110.14(C); most house equipment is 75°C, and the 90°C column is mainly a starting point for correction and adjustment. Four, apply 310.15, then check the small-conductor caps in 240.4(D): copper 14/12/10 AWG is capped at 15/20/30A, and aluminum/CCA 12/10 AWG is capped at 15/25A, no matter what the table row says.

The rows Sharma reads daily, stated as 60°C / 75°C / 90°C. Copper:
• 14 AWG — 15 / 20 / 25 A
• 12 AWG — 20 / 25 / 30 A
• 10 AWG — 30 / 35 / 40 A
• 8 AWG — 40 / 50 / 55 A
• 6 AWG — 55 / 65 / 75 A
• 4 AWG — 70 / 85 / 95 A
• 3 AWG — 85 / 100 / 115 A
• 2 AWG — 95 / 115 / 130 A
• 1/0 AWG — 125 / 150 / 170 A
• 2/0 AWG — 145 / 175 / 195 A
• 3/0 AWG — 165 / 200 / 225 A
• 4/0 AWG — 195 / 230 / 260 A
• 250 kcmil — 215 / 255 / 290 A
Aluminum and copper-clad aluminum, same format:
• 12 AWG — 15 / 20 / 25 A
• 10 AWG — 25 / 30 / 35 A
• 8 AWG — 30 / 40 / 45 A
• 6 AWG — 40 / 50 / 60 A
• 4 AWG — 55 / 65 / 75 A
• 2 AWG — 75 / 90 / 100 A
• 1/0 AWG — 100 / 120 / 135 A
• 2/0 AWG — 115 / 135 / 150 A
• 3/0 AWG — 130 / 155 / 175 A
• 4/0 AWG — 150 / 180 / 205 A
• 250 kcmil — 170 / 205 / 230 A
These are table values before 310.15 correction and adjustment, and before the 240.4(D) small-conductor caps — the caps, not the 90°C column, set the breaker on small conductors.
sections.on_the_job: Worked reads from the v1 table: 12 AWG copper is 20/25/30A at 60/75/90°C. 12 AWG CCA is 15/20/25A in the aluminum columns — and 240.4(D) caps it at a 15A breaker. 10 AWG CCA is 25/30/35A, capped at 25A. That one-column shift is exactly why a CCA circuit goes one size up from copper for the same breaker.
sections.sharma_note: S-10: branch circuits are copper by default — 14 AWG on 15A, 12 AWG on 20A. When CCA is used, go one AWG larger (12 on 15A, 10 on 20A) because Table 310.16 rates CCA in the aluminum column. Terminations must be marked for the conductor (110.14); wire connectors and lugs need AL-CU / CU-AL marking, CU-only connectors are not rated for CCA, and push-in terminals are 14 AWG solid copper only. Never backstab. The microwave circuit wire is PENDING under S-06 (12 AWG copper versus 10 AWG CCA).
sections.figure_idea: A printed Table 310.16 excerpt with the 12 AWG and 10 AWG rows highlighted, an arrow from 'CCA' into the aluminum columns, and the 240.4(D) caps written under the rows.

sections.title: CCA in every calculation — ampacity, voltage drop, fill, terminations, sizing
sections.plain_explanation: Copper-clad aluminum is a material choice inside the same calculations, not a separate code. Run every calculation the same way and pick the CCA line where the table has one: (1) Ampacity — CCA is read in the aluminum column of Table 310.16, with the 240.4(D) caps for aluminum, and the minimum conductor sizes in the cable articles apply — in 2020 work the smallest CCA branch conductor you will meet is 12 AWG, and there is no 14 AWG CCA NM. (2) Voltage drop — Chapter 9 Table 8 lists copper and aluminum resistances only; there is no CCA row, so no CCA resistance figure is given on this page for design use. A CCA voltage-drop figure has to come from the cable maker's data for the actual product, at the operating temperature. Do not use a figure worked from a resistivity class as if it were a Table 8 value. (3) Terminations — follow the identification of the actual cable and the marking and listing of the actual device, connector or lug in your hand; sources for CCA building wire do not all state the same marking rule, so check the marking before the splice and do not assume one rule fits every CCA product. Push-in backstab terminals are 14 AWG solid copper only, so CCA is never backstabbed. (4) Box fill and conduit fill — 314.16 and Chapter 9 Tables 4 and 5 go by conductor size and insulation, never by metal: a 10 AWG CCA conductor takes the same 2.50 cu in box allowance and the same Table 5 area as 10 AWG copper, and the calculation is identical; the CCA difference shows up one step earlier, in the bigger AWG the ampacity rule already chose. (5) Load calculations and service or feeder sizing — the load math (Article 220) does not change with metal; the conductor is then picked in the chosen material from Table 310.16. Whether a CCA dwelling service or whole-load feeder may be sized from the aluminum sizes in Table 310.12 has not been confirmed from the printed text — confirm it before using Table 310.12 for CCA.
sections.on_the_job: Crew version for ampacity: aluminum column, one size up. Do not use a CCA resistance in a voltage-drop calculation from this page. The 2.46 and 1.55 ohm figures here are 20°C arithmetic from a stated resistivity. They are not Chapter 9 Table 8 values, which are 75°C, and they are not verified. The calculator will not compute a CCA voltage drop until a cited 75°C source exists. Check the connector marking before the splice: if it does not say AL/CU or CC, it does not touch CCA.
sections.sharma_note: S-10 in calculation form: copper default; CCA one AWG up (12 on 15A, 10 on 20A); the microwave wire is PENDING under S-06 (12 AWG copper versus 10 AWG CCA). Sharma's CCA is Copperweld NM-B; torque CCA terminations to the printed value once — do not re-torque.
sections.figure_idea: One flow chart used five times: Load → material (Cu / Al / CCA) → column or resistance source → size → check (240.4(D) cap, fill, voltage drop), with the CCA path highlighted and the Table 8 'no CCA row' gap marked on the voltage-drop branch.
sections.florida_note: No 14 AWG CCA branch-circuit wiring in Florida 2020 work: 310.3(A) sets the minimum at 14 AWG copper or 12 AWG aluminum or copper-clad aluminum. Later editions debated 10-ampere branch circuits and 14 AWG CCA, and published sources disagree on what the 2023 edition actually adopted for 14 AWG CCA — do not rely on any later-edition 14 AWG CCA rule in 2020 work.
sections.unverified_reason: Kept unverified in the 2026-11-18 verification pass: (1) CCA voltage-drop resistance figures are derived from the ASTM B566 15 percent class maximum resistivity, not a Chapter 9 Table 8 value at 75 °C, and the class of the specific Copperweld building-wire product is not confirmed; (2) termination and device marking rules for CCA conflict between manufacturer sources; (3) sizing a CCA dwelling service or whole-load feeder from the aluminum sizes in Table 310.12 is not confirmed from the printed text; (4) published sources disagree on what the 2023 edition adopted for 14 AWG CCA and 10 A branch circuits. Page text softened so none of these points is stated as fact.

sections.title: Medium-voltage conductors and cable
sections.plain_explanation: Article 311 covers the use, installation, construction specifications and ampacities for medium-voltage conductors and cable, Type MV — a single or multiconductor solid-dielectric cable rated 2,001 volts up to and including 35,000 volts, nominal. It was new in the 2020 NEC, built from material formerly in Articles 310 and 328, and Article 328 was deleted. In the 2023 NEC this material was moved and expanded as Article 315, and Article 305, the general article for systems over 1,000 volts, is also a 2023 addition — 315 and 305 are not 2020 numbers. Sharma does not pull medium-voltage cable on ordinary work; this page exists so the book's map is complete and nobody cites the wrong edition's number.
sections.on_the_job: If a job genuinely involves Type MV cable — systems rated over 2,000 volts, up to 35,000 volts — that is engineered, utility-coordinated work — stop at this page and escalate; do not extend house habits (NM, ordinary splices, ordinary terminations) into this article.
sections.figure_idea: Single-line of a campus feeder at medium voltage with a clear 'specialized work — engineered' tag.

sections.title: Cabinets, cutout boxes and meter socket enclosures
sections.plain_explanation: Article 312 covers the enclosures the conductors in Article 310 land in: panel cabinets, cutout boxes and meter sockets. Its job is room and protection inside the enclosure — enough space to deflect and bend conductors entering the top or bottom, no sharp edges cutting insulation, doors and covers that close properly, and enclosures kept out of damp and wet locations unless they are rated for them. Working space in front of the enclosure is a Chapter 1 rule (110.26), not this article.
sections.on_the_job: On a Sharma house this is the meter enclosure and the panel cabinet. Check conductor bending room before you land a 4/0 service conductor, not after, and keep the enclosure plumb so the deadfront and door seat correctly.
sections.sharma_note: S-09 puts the meter outside and the panel inside, back to back, where the house allows — both enclosures still have to meet this article and the 110.26 working space.
sections.figure_idea: Elevation of a meter socket beside a panel cabinet with the conductor bending space shaded at the top entry.
sections.florida_note: FPL and other Florida utilities have their own meter-socket approval lists on top of the NEC — the socket must be on the serving utility's list.

sections.title: Cables entering a cabinet — and the conduit-stub exception
sections.plain_explanation: Each cable that enters a cabinet or cutout box is secured to it — the clamp or connector at the entry is what keeps a tug on the cable out of the terminations. The exception everyone uses on panel changes: where nonmetallic-sheathed cables enter the top of a surface-mounted enclosure through a raceway, the cables do not have to be individually secured to the enclosure if the raceway is not longer than 10 ft, does not penetrate a structural ceiling, each cable is fastened within 12 in — measured along the sheath — of the outer end of the raceway, and the entry is fitted to protect the cables from abrasion. Outside that exception, every cable gets its own connector and clamp.
sections.on_the_job: The stub exception is a panel-swap tool, not a rough-in shortcut: 10 ft maximum of raceway, straight into the top of the can, cables strapped within a foot of the end of the stub. If any condition fails — longer stub, or a structural ceiling in the path — each cable is secured at the enclosure like any other entry.
sections.figure_idea: Surface panel with a short conduit stub out the top: NM cables entering through it, straps marked within 12 in of the stub end, and the 10 ft limit dimensioned.

sections.title: Conductor bending and deflection space in enclosures
sections.plain_explanation:
Large conductors cannot be bent around a thumb. This section sets the minimum space inside cabinets, cutout boxes and meter enclosures for conductors to deflect and bend where they enter and land — figured from tables in the section by conductor size, number of conductors per terminal, and whether the conductor turns or runs straight through. An enclosure can be big enough on the wall and still be too small for the 4/0 or 250 kcmil that has to land in it.

Working values from Table 312.6(B) — minimum wire-bending space at terminals, one conductor per terminal:
• 4/0 AWG — 5-1/2 in
• 250 kcmil — 6 in
• 300 kcmil — 6-1/2 in
• 350 kcmil — 7 in
• 400 kcmil — 8 in
• 500 kcmil — 8 in
• 600 kcmil — 9 in
• 750 kcmil — 10 in
• 1000 kcmil — 12 in
Two conductors landing on one terminal need more than the one-conductor figure — the table's next columns. Deflection space for conductors that enter and turn inside the gutter is Table 312.6(A), figured separately.
sections.on_the_job: Size the enclosure from the conductor, not the wall space: check the bending-space table for the largest conductor and the entry direction (top, bottom, side) before the gear is ordered. Forcing a feeder into too-tight a bend is damaged insulation and a failed inspection in one move.
sections.figure_idea: Panel interior with a large feeder conductor bending from a bottom entry to its lug, the required bending space shaded and dimensioned from the section's table (values left to the table, not restated).

sections.title: What may live inside an enclosure for switches and overcurrent devices
sections.plain_explanation: An enclosure that houses switches or overcurrent devices is not a general-purpose junction box, but it is not sealed against all other wiring either: this section allows conductors to run through and splice inside it within set limits — commonly taught as the wiring space used by feed-through conductors being limited to a share of the enclosure's cross-sectional wiring space (40%), and splices and taps to a larger share (75%), with the exact conditions in the section. The 2020 changes also addressed power-monitoring and energy-management equipment installed in these enclosures.
sections.on_the_job: Do not treat a panel as free splice space on a remodel. If feed-through or splices are planned in an overcurrent enclosure, count the space, keep it in the wiring gutter area, and be ready to show the inspector the section you relied on.
sections.figure_idea: Panel gutter detail with feed-through conductors occupying a measured share of the wiring space, splice bundle tagged separately.

sections.title: Outlet, device, pull and junction boxes
sections.plain_explanation: Article 314 is the box article: which box, how big, how it is set, how it is supported, and what may live in it. The sizing heart is 314.16 — a box is big enough only if its marked volume holds every conductor, device, clamp and ground the counting rules charge against it. The placement rules around it (setback, repair, support, fan rating, accessibility) are what inspectors check after the volume math passes.
sections.on_the_job: Run the fill math before the rough-in, not at trim. A box that fails fill in the wall fails the same way on paper — cheaper to catch it on paper.
sections.figure_idea: Cutaway of a 4-square box with a receptacle, two NM cables and clamps, each counted item tagged 1x, 2x or 'grounds = 1'.

sections.title: Box fill — volume, allowances and counting
sections.plain_explanation:
A box may not be filled past its volume. Start with the box volume: for a standard metal box use Table 314.16(A); for a nonmetallic or marked box use the volume marked on the box itself. Then charge the contents using Table 314.16(B) allowances — 2.00 cu in for each 14 AWG, 2.25 for each 12 AWG, 2.50 for each 10 AWG. The counting rules in 314.16(B)(1) through (5) decide how many allowances each thing costs — including the 2020 grounds rule on the next page (up to four grounds count once, each one past four adds a quarter) — and the total charge may not exceed the box volume.

Box volumes from Table 314.16(A) for the boxes Sharma stocks:
• 4 in square × 1-1/2 in deep — 21.0 cu in
• 4 in square × 2-1/8 in deep — 30.3 cu in
• 4-11/16 in square × 1-1/2 in deep — 25.5 cu in
• 4-11/16 in square × 2-1/8 in deep — 42.0 cu in
• 4 in octagonal × 1-1/4 in deep — 12.5 cu in
• 4 in octagonal × 1-1/2 in deep — 15.0 cu in
• 4 in octagonal × 2-1/8 in deep — 21.5 cu in
A plaster ring or extension ring marked with its volume adds that volume; an unmarked one adds nothing you may count.
sections.on_the_job: The five counts, in field order: (1) each conductor that enters from outside and ends or is spliced in the box counts once, and a conductor that passes through unbroken also counts once, while a short pigtail that starts and ends in the box counts zero; (2) [see the (B) page for the full list in order]. Worked example from the v1 tables: a 4 x 1-1/2 square box is 21.0 cu in. Three 12/2 NM cables, one receptacle and internal clamps charge 6 conductors x 2.25 = 13.50, grounds 2.25, device yoke 4.50, clamps 2.25 — total 22.50 cu in. It fails. The 4 x 2-1/8 square at 30.3 cu in passes.
sections.sharma_note: Box height on the wall is not a 314 rule — Sharma S-04 (receptacles 18 in to the bottom of the box, plan silent) and S-05 (switches 48 in to center) govern placement; 314 governs whether the box you placed is big enough and set right.
sections.figure_idea: Worksheet-style figure: left side a box volume stamp '30.3 cu in', right side a tally list adding to 22.50, with a green check.

sections.title: The five counting rules, one by one
sections.plain_explanation: 314.16(B)(1) Conductors: each conductor from outside the box that is spliced or terminated counts once; a conductor that runs through unbroken counts once; an unbroken loop or coil of conductor not less than twice the minimum free-conductor length required by 300.14 — so 12 in or more of loop — counts twice; pigtails that originate in the box count zero. (B)(2) Clamps: where one or more internal cable clamps are present, all of them together count once, at the largest conductor in the box; a cable connector with its clamping mechanism outside the box counts zero. (B)(3) Support fittings: where luminaire studs or hickeys are present, count one allowance for each type of fitting — all studs together count once, and all hickeys together count once, so a box with both a stud and a hickey counts two — at the largest conductor in the box. (B)(4) Devices: each device yoke or strap counts twice, at the largest conductor connected to that device; a device wider than a single 2 in device box counts twice for each gang required to mount it. (B)(5) Grounds — the count that changed in 2020: up to four equipment grounding conductors and equipment bonding jumpers entering the box together count once, at the largest ground in the box, and each additional one beyond four adds a quarter of that allowance. Isolated-ground conductors count in with the rest of the grounds; the old separate extra allowance for an isolated-ground set is a 2017 rule and does not apply in 2020.
sections.on_the_job: Say the counts out loud as you tally: wires, clamps, studs, yokes, grounds. Field example at 12 AWG (2.25 cu in): four grounds = 2.25 cu in; six grounds = 2.25 + (2 x 0.25 x 2.25) = 3.38 cu in. In a normal house box with two or three cables the ground count is four or fewer, so the old habit gives the same answer — the quarter rule only bites in crowded multi-cable boxes, which is exactly where fill was already tight.
sections.figure_idea: Five-row tally card with icons: conductor, clamp, stud, yoke, ground bar, each with its multiplier.
sections.florida_note: The 2020 quarter-allowance count is what this page, the calculator, the starter quiz, and lookup L-064 now teach. The printed 2020 text of 314.16(B)(5) was checked in the 2026-11-18 verification pass. The old 'all grounds count as one, however many' rule is the 2017 rule.

sections.title: Conduit bodies — fill and splices
sections.plain_explanation: Conduit bodies follow fill rules too. The conductors inside a conduit body may not exceed the fill the Chapter 9 tables allow for the raceway size the body belongs to. Splices, taps, and devices are allowed inside a conduit body only where the body is durably and legibly marked with its cubic-inch capacity by the manufacturer — and then the fill is counted the same way box fill is counted, against that marked volume. An unmarked LB is a pulling fitting, not a junction box: no splices live in it.
sections.on_the_job: Read the casting before you splice: no cubic-inch marking, no splice. If the job needs a splice at that point, the fix is a marked body or a real box — not a bigger wirenut.
sections.figure_idea: Two conduit bodies: one cast with its cubic-inch capacity marked, holding a splice (approved); one unmarked with a splice inside (crossed out).

sections.title: Conductors and cables entering boxes
sections.plain_explanation: Cables entering a box have to be secured to it, or the cable has to be fastened close enough that the box entry stays put, and the cable sheath has to continue into the box so the conductors are protected where they enter. The v1 field rule (L-065): the sheath extends at least 1/4 in inside the box past any clamp, and with single-gang nonmetallic boxes the cable is fastened within 8 in of the box while the sheath still goes 1/4 in in.
sections.on_the_job: Strip the sheath outside the box, not inside it: 1/4 in of sheath past the clamp is protection; 2 in of sheath inside the box is fill you did not count and a make-up fight at trim.
sections.figure_idea: Close-up of an NM cable entering a plastic box: sheath ending 1/4 in past the knockout, conductors separating after that point.

sections.title: How a box sits in a wall or ceiling
sections.plain_explanation: How far a box may sit behind the finished surface depends on what that surface is made of. In concrete, tile, gypsum board (drywall), plaster, or other noncombustible material, the front of the box, plaster ring, extension ring, or listed extender may be back no more than 1/4 inch. In wood or other combustible material, the box or extender has to reach the finished surface or project past it. Drywall is noncombustible for this rule even when it is screwed to wood studs. A box buried farther than the rule allows is both a device problem — the yoke ears cannot reach — and a code problem.
sections.on_the_job: Set box depth off the stud face for the finish that is actually going on that wall: 1/2 in drywall is not tile on backer board. Use the adjustable-depth or extension option before the wall closes, not a stack of goof rings at trim.
sections.sharma_note: S-04 and S-05 set the height (18 in to bottom for receptacles, 48 in to center for switches, plan silent); this section sets the depth. Both have to be right on the same box.
sections.figure_idea: Wall section: stud, drywall, and a box face drawn flush, with a second box drawn 1/4 in back marked 'noncombustible only'.

sections.title: Repairing the surface around a box
sections.plain_explanation: Where a box is set in a noncombustible wall or ceiling, the broken or chipped surface around it has to be repaired so there is no gap or open space bigger than 1/8 in around the box. The plate cannot be the patch — the surface itself has to come back to the box.
sections.on_the_job: On remodel work, check the gap before you set the device. A 1/4 in crater around a cut-in box is a fail here and a wobbly device later; use the right box or repair the opening.

sections.title: Supporting boxes
sections.plain_explanation: A box has to be supported — screwed, nailed, braced or hung by a method the article allows for that box type — rigidly enough that it does not move when devices are plugged in and pulled out for twenty years. Surface boxes, pendant boxes and boxes in walls and ceilings each have their own allowed supports in this section, and a box supported by a raceway alone is allowed only in the narrow cases the section describes.
sections.on_the_job: Wiggle test at rough-in: grab the box and push. If it moves, the device will move at trim and the plate will never sit flat. Add the brace or bracket now.

sections.title: Boxes at lighting outlets — the 50-pound rule
sections.plain_explanation: A box used at a lighting outlet has to be listed for the purpose, and it may support a luminaire (or lampholder) weighing up to 50 lb. A heavier luminaire may be supported by the box only where the box is listed and marked for the weight it will actually carry; otherwise the fixture is supported independently of the box. Ceiling fans are not luminaires under this rule — a fan needs a fan-rated box under 314.27(C), even if the fan weighs less than 50 lb.
sections.on_the_job: Big foyer and lanai fixtures are the trap: weigh the fixture or look up its weight before trim-out. Over 50 lb with no weight marking on the box means an independent support — plan it at rough-in, not with the fixture hanging from your lift.
sections.figure_idea: Ceiling box with a 45 lb fixture (approved), a 65 lb fixture on an unmarked box (crossed out), and the same fixture on an independent support (approved).

sections.title: Boxes at ceiling-fan outlets
sections.plain_explanation: Where an outlet in a habitable room ceiling is in a spot that could support a ceiling fan — wired and placed the way a fan location is — the box has to be listed for fan support, and the maximum weight it may carry is marked on it. A fan over 35 lb up to 70 lb needs a box marked for that weight; a fan heavier than 70 lb is supported independently of the box.
sections.on_the_job: If there is a ceiling outlet in a bedroom or living room with a switch leg, rough it in with a fan-rated box whether or not the plan shows a fan today — the next owner will hang one there. That is checklist BL-09.
sections.figure_idea: Ceiling box seen from below with its fan-support marking enlarged, and a fan outline above it.

sections.title: Pull and junction boxes for conductors 4 AWG and larger
sections.plain_explanation: Once conductors reach 4 AWG and larger, box sizing stops being a cubic-inch question and becomes a geometry question: the box must be big enough to pull and bend stiff conductors without damaging them. For a straight pull — in one wall, out the opposite wall — the distance from the entry to the opposite wall must be at least eight times the trade size of the largest raceway. For an angle pull, a U pull or splices, that distance must be at least six times the largest raceway in the row, plus the sum of the trade sizes of the other raceways in the same row on the same wall; and the distance between raceways that enclose the same conductor must be at least six times the larger raceway. These rules are in 314.28(A)(1) and (A)(2).
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: a straight pull with a largest raceway of 2 in needs at least 16 in from entry to opposite wall. An angle pull in a row with a 2 in and a 1 in raceway needs at least (6 x 2) + 1 = 13 in to the opposite wall. Cubic inches do not rescue a box that fails this geometry.
sections.figure_idea: Two plan-view box diagrams side by side: straight pull dimensioned 8x, angle pull dimensioned 6x + sum of the row.

sections.title: Boxes must stay accessible
sections.plain_explanation: A junction or pull box has to remain accessible without removing any part of the building — no drywall, no tile, no fixed cabinetry over the cover. If reaching the splice means cutting the building open, the box was in the wrong place when the walls were open.
sections.on_the_job: Before close-in, walk the job and photograph every junction box location. If a cover will be behind a fixed finish, move the box or move the splice now.

sections.title: Armored cable — Type AC
sections.plain_explanation: Type AC is a factory cable with its conductors inside a flexible metal armor, with an internal bonding strip in contact with the armor so the armor can serve as the equipment ground path. Sharma meets this article most often through one cross-reference: 334.23 sends NM cable in accessible attics to the attic protection rules written here in 320.23. The cable itself shows up on Sharma jobs mainly in older work and the occasional commercial job.
sections.on_the_job: Do not confuse AC with MC: AC carries its bonding strip and uses fittings listed for AC; MC (Article 330) usually carries a separate green ground conductor. The fittings are not interchangeable by habit — use the fitting listed for the cable in your hand.
sections.figure_idea: Detail of AC cable end: armor, bonding strip folded back, anti-short bushing at the connector.

sections.title: Flat cable assemblies — Type FC
sections.plain_explanation: Type FC is a factory flat-cable assembly of parallel conductors formed integrally with an insulating web, made to be field-installed in a surface metal raceway identified for the use — a specialized method, not a substitute for NM run loose in a wall. It is permitted only as branch circuits, with a branch-circuit rating not exceeding 30 amperes, to supply suitable tap devices for lighting, small appliances, or small power loads, where installed for exposed work in locations where it will not be subject to physical damage, and protected by a cover identified for the use where it is installed less than 8 ft above the floor or a fixed working platform. The cable, raceway, tap devices and fittings are a listed system, installed by this article and the manufacturer's instructions.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma does not install Type FC on ordinary work. If a spec calls for it, the listed system components come as a set — do not mix in ordinary boxes or fittings.

sections.title: Flat conductor cable — Type FCC
sections.plain_explanation: Type FCC is a flat conductor cable system designed to be installed under carpet squares and similar finishes, with its own shields, boxes and transition fittings. It is a different method from Type FC flat cable assemblies (Article 322) — the two are not interchangeable, and neither is ordinary branch wiring in a flat jacket.
sections.on_the_job: Encountered almost only in specialized commercial fit-outs. Identify the system by its listing before touching an existing FCC installation.

sections.title: Integrated gas spacer cable — Type IGS
sections.plain_explanation: Type IGS is a specialized underground cable: a factory assembly of one or more individually insulated conductors — solid aluminum rods laid parallel — enclosed in a loose-fit nonmetallic flexible conduit, insulated with dry kraft paper and pressurized sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) gas, and rated 0 through 600 volts. It is a below-grade method for service conductors, feeders, and branch circuits, including direct earth burial. It must not be used as interior wiring, must not be exposed in contact with a building, and must not be used above ground. It exists in the book so the map is complete, far outside house and light-commercial branch work.
sections.on_the_job: No Sharma field use. If IGS appears on a drawing, it is an engineered system — escalate, do not substitute a familiar cable.

sections.title: Metal-clad cable — Type MC
sections.plain_explanation:
Type MC is a factory assembly of insulated conductors inside a metal sheath — smooth, corrugated or interlocked armor — with its own equipment grounding arrangement. It is the commercial counterpart to NM: it can be used exposed or concealed, in dry locations and the other locations its listing allows, fished in existing walls, and run where NM cannot go, such as many commercial ceilings and walls. It may not be used where it will be subject to physical damage, in wet locations unless the specific cable is listed for it, or in the other prohibited uses its article lists.

The support numbers (330.30): MC must be secured within 12 in of every box, cabinet, and fitting, and supported at intervals not exceeding 6 ft. Short lengths to luminaires and fished runs in existing walls have their own exceptions in that section — the 12 in and 6 ft figures are the default rhythm.
sections.on_the_job: Cut MC with the right tool and use listed MC connectors — a Romex connector is not an MC connector. Support and securing follow 330.30 (see the companion lookup), with the familiar pattern of securing close to boxes and supporting at regular intervals, plus exceptions for fished runs and short lengths to luminaires.
sections.sharma_note: S-01 applies on commercial work, where MC is most used: 20A minimum branch circuits, 12 AWG copper minimum.
sections.figure_idea: MC cable run across commercial studs with a listed connector at a 4-square box, armor and green ground shown.

sections.title: Where MC may — and may not — be used
sections.plain_explanation: Type MC is the commercial workhorse because its list of permitted uses is long: exposed or concealed, in dry locations, in cable tray, fished into existing walls and ceilings, and in wet locations where the specific cable assembly is listed for it — an impervious jacket or corrosion-resistant construction is what makes an MC cable wet-location legal; plain interlocked armor is not. The not-permitted list is shorter but firm: MC may not be used where subject to physical damage, it is not a direct-burial cable unless the specific cable is identified for burial, and it may not be embedded in concrete or aggregate unless identified for it. Read the jacket print: the ratings live on the cable, not in the article's title.
sections.on_the_job: Before MC leaves the shop, match the jacket print to the location: wet location, tray, plenum — each is a marking on the actual cable. 'MC is MC' is how a dry-location cable ends up in a damp mechanical room and fails inspection.
sections.figure_idea: Three MC reels with jacket legends highlighted: standard interlocked (dry), jacketed and wet-location listed, and tray rated, each with its location tag.

sections.title: Securing and supporting MC cable
sections.plain_explanation:
MC is secured within 12 in of each box, cabinet, or fitting, and supported at intervals of not more than 6 ft. The exceptions carry the field cases:
• Fished through existing walls or ceilings — no securing required where the cable cannot be reached
• A length of not more than 6 ft from the last point of support to a luminaire or other equipment within an accessible ceiling — the ceiling whip
• Short lengths at terminals where flexibility is needed for equipment that moves or vibrates
Outside those cases, a long unsupported drape of MC across a ceiling is a violation even if it happens to be resting on the grid.
sections.on_the_job: Strap MC like you mean it: within a foot of the box, then every 6 ft or less, with straps that fit the cable. The 6 ft whip allowance is measured from the last real support — not from wherever the cable happened to leave the bundle.
sections.figure_idea: MC run above a ceiling: strap at 12 in from the box, supports dimensioned at 6 ft, and a 6 ft whip dropping to a lay-in fixture.

sections.title: Mineral-insulated, metal-sheathed cable — Type MI
sections.plain_explanation: Type MI is a copper or alloy sheath packed with mineral insulation around its conductors — a cable chosen where extreme heat, fire survival or mechanical abuse rules out ordinary methods, such as fire-pump and critical circuits and harsh industrial spots. Its terminations are specialized sealed fittings, and moisture control at the ends is part of the installation, not an afterthought.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma meets MI mainly as existing work in older or specialized installations. Do not cut or terminate it with NM/MC habits — the sealing fitting and its instructions govern.

sections.title: Nonmetallic-sheathed cable — Types NM, NMC, NMS (Romex)
sections.plain_explanation: This is Sharma's house cable. NM is two or more insulated conductors with an equipment ground, factory-wrapped in a nonmetallic sheath. Article 334 says where it may be used (334.10), where it may never be used (334.12), how it is protected and run (334.15, 334.17, 334.23), how it is bent (334.24), how often it is secured and supported (334.30), and how its ampacity is limited (334.80). Almost every Sharma rough-in decision — staple spacing, attic runs, the 60°C ampacity limit — traces back to this one article.
sections.on_the_job: If you learn one article in this chapter cold, learn this one. The other methods are variations; NM is the daily work.
sections.figure_idea: A coil of 12/2 NM beside a stapled stud bay run, with callouts to 334.30 (staples), 334.15 (protection) and 334.80 (ampacity).

sections.title: Where NM may be used
sections.plain_explanation: NM may be used exposed or concealed in normally dry locations, in one- and two-family dwellings and their garages, and in the other buildings and construction types this section allows. 'Normally dry' is the load-bearing phrase: the cable is a dry-location method, and the building type limits in this section are why a method that is fine in a house may not be fine in a larger commercial building.
sections.on_the_job: House, garage and accessory work in dry interiors: NM is the default. Anything wet, damp, underground or in a bigger occupancy: stop and check 334.12 and pick another method.

sections.title: Where NM may not be used
sections.plain_explanation: NM may not be used in wet or damp locations — including inside a raceway that is itself underground or outdoors, because the inside of that raceway is a wet location — as service-entrance cable, embedded in concrete or masonry, in areas subject to physical damage without protection, or in the other locations this section lists. It is a dry, protected, interior method.
sections.on_the_job: The classic fail: NM sleeved in PVC down an outside wall and underground to a yard light. The PVC does not make the location dry. Use UF or conductors in raceway for that run (Articles 340 and 352).
sections.figure_idea: Red-X diagram: NM entering an underground PVC run; green-check diagram beside it with UF cable on the same route.
sections.florida_note: Florida's humidity does not reclassify an interior dry location, but any exterior or underground raceway interior is wet — plan the method for the location, not the weather.

sections.title: NM in exposed work and through framing
sections.plain_explanation: Exposed NM has to follow the surface it is run on and be protected where it can be hit. Where it passes through a floor, a wall or framing, the Article 300 protection rules ride along: bored-hole setbacks and nail plates from 300.4, and protection where the cable passes through slots or notches. In unfinished basements and crawl spaces, this section sets how larger cables may run through joists and how smaller cables are run on running boards or through bored holes. The basement and crawl-space case has its own subsection, 334.15(C): where cable runs at angles with the joists, a cable at least as large as two 6 AWG or three 8 AWG conductors may be secured directly to the lower edges of the joists; smaller cables must run through bored holes in the joists or on running boards. NM on the wall of an unfinished basement must be protected — in listed conduit or tubing, or protected the way 300.4 requires — with a bushing or adapter where the cable enters the raceway.
sections.on_the_job: Treat an unfinished basement ceiling like a wall someone will finish later: bore the joists or use running boards, keep the cable tight to the framing, and plate anything in the strike zone.
sections.figure_idea: Basement joist bay with NM bored through joist centers and a smaller cable on a running board, both labeled.

sections.title: NM in accessible attics — the scuttle rule
sections.plain_explanation: For accessible attics, this section points NM cable at the attic rules written for AC cable in 320.23: 334.23 says the installation of cable in accessible attics or roof spaces shall also comply with 320.23. Under 320.23(A), cable run across the top of floor joists, or within 7 ft of the floor or floor joists across the face of rafters or studding, has to be protected by substantial guard strips that are at least as high as the cable; where the space is not accessible by permanent stairs or ladders, that protection is required only within 6 ft of the nearest edge of the scuttle hole or attic entrance. Under 320.23(B), cable installed parallel to the sides of rafters, studs, or ceiling or floor joists needs neither guard strips nor running boards, and the installation must also comply with 300.4(D). Sanjay's own ruling in the Sharma note is separate company practice — stricter and simpler than the code rule — and it is what Sharma crews follow on Sharma jobs.
sections.on_the_job: Route attic runs the Sharma way from the start and the inspection question mostly disappears: runs hug the framing, nothing crosses the scuttle opening, and nothing invites a foot.
sections.sharma_note: SHARMA RULE (Sanjay, definitive 2026-11-09 — company practice, not a code quote): within 6 ft of an attic scuttle with no permanent stairs, run NM along the sides of the joists/trusses only, parallel to the framing, never diagonally across it and never across the opening; no guard strips; bends stay at least 1.5 ft clear of the opening; the attic light sits about 1.5 ft beside the opening with its switch at the entry. This is how BuzzDraws and the crews run it, regardless of how the 320.23 wording settles.
sections.figure_idea: Plan view of a scuttle opening with a 6 ft band shaded around it, NM runs drawn parallel along joist sides inside the band, one diagonal run crossed out.

sections.title: Bending radius of NM cable
sections.plain_explanation: NM may not be bent so sharply that the bend damages the sheath or the conductors inside it; the rule of this section is expressed as a minimum radius measured to the inner edge of the bend — commonly taught as five times the cable diameter. A kinked flat cable at a tight stud turn is exactly the damage this section is aimed at.
sections.on_the_job: Make wide, lazy turns. If you have to force it around a corner with your thumb creasing the sheath, the bend is too tight — re-route or move the hole.

sections.title: Securing and supporting NM
sections.plain_explanation: NM must be secured and supported at intervals not exceeding 4-1/2 ft, and within 12 in of every box, cabinet and fitting. Cable run through bored holes or notches in framing counts as secured and supported by that framing. Flat cable may not be stapled on edge, and the staple has to hold the cable snug without crushing the sheath.
sections.on_the_job: Staple pattern on a stud run: within 12 in of the box, then at least every 4-1/2 ft, snug not crushed. A staple that deforms the sheath is a damage point, not a support point.
sections.figure_idea: Stud bay with staple positions dimensioned: 12 in max from the box, 4 ft 6 in max between staples.

sections.title: Ampacity of NM cable — the 60°C limit
sections.plain_explanation: The conductors inside NM are 90°C rated, but the cable's ampacity is limited to the 60°C column of Table 310.16. You may still start correction and adjustment math from the 90°C value — that is what makes a bundled or hot-attic NM run survivable on paper — as long as the final ampacity after 310.15 does not exceed the 60°C value, and the 240.4(D) small-conductor caps still apply on top.
sections.on_the_job: Field translation: 14 AWG NM on a 15A breaker and 12 AWG NM on a 20A breaker, full stop — and if you derate a bundle of home runs, do the math from 90°C, then cap the answer at the 60°C column (20A for 12 AWG — the same place the 240.4(D) breaker cap lands).
sections.sharma_note: S-10 still governs the wire choice: copper by default; CCA one size up. NM ampacity limits apply the same either way, read in the correct 310.16 column for the metal.
sections.figure_idea: Two-column mini-table: 12 AWG NM — 90°C start 30A (Cu) for derating, 60°C final cap 20A, breaker cap 20A.
sections.unverified_reason: Corrected 2026-11-25: this page previously stated the 60°C cap for 12 AWG NM as 25A; Table 310.16 gives 20A at 60°C for 12 AWG copper (25A is the 75°C column). Flagged for Mike Holt re-check after the correction.

sections.title: Power and control tray cable — Type TC
sections.plain_explanation: Type TC is a factory assembly of power or control conductors with an overall jacket, listed for installation in cable tray (Article 392) and the other uses its article permits. Tray-rated is the load-bearing word: a cable in a tray must be a cable type Article 392 allows, and TC is the common one. Certain TC constructions carry additional ratings (such as exposed-run ratings) only when the cable is marked for them.
sections.on_the_job: On a light-commercial tray job, read the jacket print before the cable leaves the shop: TC alone is not every rating — check for the marking that matches the actual installation.

sections.title: Type P cable
sections.plain_explanation: Type P is a rugged, flexible cable construction originating in marine and drilling work, listed in the 2020 NEC for the applications its article describes, including certain hazardous-location uses noted in the 2020 changes. It is not a house or ordinary commercial branch-circuit cable.
sections.on_the_job: No Sharma field use on ordinary work. Its presence on a drawing signals a specialized, engineered specification.

sections.title: Service-entrance cable — Types SE and USE
sections.plain_explanation: Type SE cable is a single-conductor or multi-conductor assembly, primarily used for services. Type SE has a flame-retardant, moisture-resistant covering and is the above-ground form. Type USE is identified for underground use, has a moisture-resistant covering, but is not required to have a flame-retardant covering. On a house, SE is the cable that can carry the service where individual conductors in a mast or raceway are not used. Where SE is used for interior branch-circuit or feeder wiring, 338.10(B)(4) makes the Article 334 installation rules apply to that run — see the 338.10(B)(4) page. Type SE and Type USE are not interchangeable: SE shall not be used underground, with or without a raceway, and USE shall not be used for interior wiring. A cable that is also marked and listed as another wiring type is used indoors under that other rating, not as USE.
sections.on_the_job: Keep service work in its own lane: conductor sizing is 310.12 / 310.16 work, the disconnect and grounding live in Chapters 2 and 2/250 territory, and this article governs the cable itself.
sections.sharma_note: S-02: new meter-mains and disconnects are Siemens. S-09: meter and panel back to back where the house allows.
sections.figure_idea: House elevation: service drop to a mast, SE cable down through the meter to an inside panel.
sections.florida_note: The serving utility (FPL and the Florida co-ops/munis) controls the drop, meter and its own connection rules on top of the NEC.

sections.title: SE cable used as interior wiring
sections.plain_explanation: Type SE cable is a service-entrance cable first, but 338.10(B)(4) also lets it be used as interior wiring for branch circuits and feeders inside a building. When it is used that way, the installation has to follow Part II of Article 334 for NM cable — excluding 334.80. The routing, protection and support rules of Part II therefore apply to the indoor SE run, but the NM ampacity rule in 334.80 does not. SE has its own narrow ampacity rule instead: for ungrounded conductor sizes 10 AWG and smaller, where installed in contact with thermal insulation, the ampacity is in accordance with the 60°C conductor temperature rating.
sections.on_the_job: An SE cable feeding a subpanel inside the house is roughed and protected like Romex once it is indoors: bored-hole and notch protection, and the Article 334 support intervals, travel with it. The 334.80 ampacity cap does not — 338.10(B)(4)(a) excludes 334.80. Size the conductors from Article 310, and apply the 60°C column only where 338.10(B)(4) itself requires it: ungrounded conductors 10 AWG and smaller in contact with thermal insulation.

sections.title: Where SE and USE cable may not be used
sections.plain_explanation: The prohibitions keep service cable in its lane. Type USE is an underground cable: it may not be used for interior wiring, and not aboveground at all, except where it terminates inside listed equipment it is permitted to enter. Type SE may not be used underground (that is USE's job), and SE used as interior branch-circuit or feeder wiring is limited to the conditions on the 338.10(B)(4) page — outside those conditions, interior circuits get an interior wiring method. Service cable leaving the meter is service territory; it does not become a general-purpose house cable because it was on the truck.
sections.on_the_job: The classic misuse is USE pulled inside a building 'because it was already in the trench.' Once the run comes inside, the method has to change to one that is legal indoors — plan the transition at the entry, in a box or the panel, not mid-run.
sections.figure_idea: House wall section: USE stopping at the entry point and transitioning to an interior method (approved), versus USE continuing across the attic (crossed out).

sections.title: Underground feeder cable — Type UF
sections.plain_explanation: UF is NM's underground sibling: the conductors are embedded in a solid moisture-resistant covering so the cable itself is rated for direct burial and wet locations, and for sunlight exposure where it is marked sunlight resistant. It is used for yard lights, outbuildings, pool and landscape feeds and other underground branch circuits and feeders, buried at the cover depth Article 300.5 sets for it — 24 in for direct burial in the general case, with the 12 in residential GFCI exception L-061 teaches.
sections.on_the_job: UF is stiff and unforgiving to strip — score the covering carefully and do not nick the conductors. Above ground, protect it where it can be damaged, the same as any exposed cable, and sleeve risers where 300.5 requires protection.
sections.figure_idea: Trench detail: UF at 24 in with a sleeved riser at the house wall, warning about the 12 in GFCI residential exception noted as a separate case.

sections.title: Where UF may — and may not — be used
sections.plain_explanation: UF's permitted list is the underground counterpart to NM's: direct burial, wet locations, corrosive locations, and sunlight exposure where the cable is marked sunlight resistant. Where UF is used in place of NM for a branch circuit, it is installed under the NM framework it points to (Article 334's protection and support rules). The not-permitted list keeps it out of service work and buildings it does not belong in: UF may not be used as service-entrance cable, in commercial garages, theaters and similar locations, motion picture studios, storage battery rooms, or hoistways, and not embedded in poured concrete or left exposed to physical damage without protection.
sections.on_the_job: Yard lights and outbuilding feeds are UF's home turf — but the moment the feed becomes the building's service, UF is the wrong cable. And like NM, its ampacity is read at the 60°C limit (340.80), so size it the way the 334.80 page teaches.
sections.figure_idea: Yard cross-section: UF buried to a pedestal light (approved); UF rising into a meter base as a service cable (crossed out).

sections.title: Intermediate metal conduit — IMC
sections.plain_explanation:
IMC is the middle-weight steel raceway: thinner wall than rigid metal conduit, heavier and stronger than EMT, threaded like RMC and usable in most of the same places, including many wet and exposed locations with the right fittings. Sharma meets it mainly on commercial and service work where EMT is not tough enough and full rigid is not needed.

The support numbers (342.30): IMC must be fastened within 3 ft of each box, cabinet, conduit body, or other termination. For straight runs, Table 342.30(B)(2) spaces supports by size:
• 1/2 in and 3/4 in — every 10 ft
• 1 in — every 12 ft
• 1-1/4 in and 1-1/2 in — every 14 ft
• 2 in — every 16 ft
• 2-1/2 in and larger — every 20 ft
sections.on_the_job: One trade size note that matters in the field: IMC and RMC share the same outside diameter, but IMC's thinner wall gives it a larger inside area, so its Chapter 9, Table 4 fill values are its own — do not use the RMC row for an IMC run. Link to Chapter 9 for the actual numbers; do not re-derive them here.
sections.figure_idea: Three short raceway stubs side by side — EMT, IMC, RMC — wall thickness shown in cross-section.

sections.title: Rigid metal conduit — RMC
sections.plain_explanation:
RMC is the heavy-wall threaded steel raceway — the toughest common raceway in this chapter. It may be used in nearly every location, including underground (where its 6 in cover in the general open-ground row of Table 300.5 is the payoff for its strength. Under a one- or two-family dwelling driveway that same rigid metal conduit needs 18 in, the same as PVC and direct-burial cable. Streets, roads, and other driveways and parking lots demand 24 in for every method), wet locations, and places subject to physical damage, with fittings and supports made for it. Underground, corrosion protection and the soil conditions govern how long it lasts.

The support numbers (344.30): RMC must be fastened within 3 ft of each box, cabinet, conduit body, or other termination — with the section's allowances where threaded couplings make that impractical. For straight runs, Table 344.30(B)(2) spaces supports by size:
• 1/2 in and 3/4 in — every 10 ft
• 1 in — every 12 ft
• 1-1/4 in and 1-1/2 in — every 14 ft
• 2 in — every 16 ft
• 2-1/2 in and larger — every 20 ft
sections.on_the_job: The 6 in burial depth is why RMC still earns its cost in open ground and in shallow-rock trenches that are not under a driveway. It is not a 6 in depth under a one- or two-family dwelling driveway — that row is 18 in for RMC and for PVC. Under streets, roads, alleys, and other driveways or parking lots, Table 300.5 requires 24 in of cover for every method, RMC included.
sections.figure_idea: Open-ground cross-section: RMC at 6 in beside a PVC run at 18 in. A one- or two-family dwelling driveway is a different Table 300.5 row — 18 in for both.

sections.title: Flexible metal conduit — FMC ('Greenfield')
sections.plain_explanation:
FMC is a flexible spiral metal raceway used for short, bendy final connections — inside equipment, across a vibration gap, or fished where a rigid method cannot go. It is not a wet-location method in its basic form (that is LFMC, Article 350), it needs fittings listed for it, and when it is used as the ground path its length and overcurrent limits are restricted — on Sharma work, pull a green ground and do not rely on the spiral.

The working numbers (348.30 and 348.60): FMC is fastened within 12 in of each termination and supported at intervals not over 4-1/2 ft, with exceptions for lengths fished in existing construction, for up to 3 ft at a terminal where flexibility is needed after installation, and for a whip of up to 6 ft to a luminaire in an accessible ceiling. As a grounding path, the spiral itself counts only where the fittings are listed for grounding, the total length in the ground return path is not over 6 ft, and the circuit's overcurrent protection stays within the limits this article sets for the trade size (20 amperes for 3/8 in and 1/2 in). Sharma practice stays ahead of all of this: pull the green ground.
sections.on_the_job: Keep FMC whips short and supported, bond with a real conductor, and switch to LFMC the moment the location is wet or outdoors.

sections.title: Liquidtight flexible metal conduit — LFMC
sections.plain_explanation:
LFMC is FMC with a liquidtight plastic jacket over the metal core — the flexible method for wet locations, outdoors, and vibrating equipment. On Sharma work this is the condenser whip: LFMC from the disconnect to the outdoor unit, with listed liquidtight fittings, supported close to each end, and a separate equipment ground inside.
