The working numbers (350.30 and 350.60): LFMC is fastened within 12 in of each termination and supported at intervals not over 4-1/2 ft; a length of up to 6 ft is permitted unsupported at a luminaire or equipment connection within an accessible ceiling, and short lengths at terminals may go unsupported where flexibility is needed. As a grounding path, the jacketed spiral counts only in trade sizes 3/8 in through 1-1/4 in, with listed fittings, a total ground-path length not over 6 ft, and the overcurrent limits this article sets — which is why the condenser whip still gets its own equipment grounding conductor inside, sized from Table 250.122.
sections.on_the_job: The whip is not the support for the disconnect and the disconnect is not the support for the whip — strap both, keep the whip off the ground where it will be weed-eaten, and seal the outdoor end with the listed fitting, hand-tight plus the manufacturer's turn, not channel-locks.
sections.figure_idea: Condenser pad detail: disconnect on the wall, LFMC whip looping down to the unit with support straps marked.
sections.florida_note: 210.8(F) GFCI enforcement on outdoor HVAC outlets has varied by AHJ and amendment — see the Chapter 2 note; confirm locally before choosing the condenser breaker.

sections.title: Rigid polyvinyl chloride conduit — PVC
sections.plain_explanation:
PVC is the nonmetallic rigid raceway Sharma uses underground and in wet and corrosive spots: services and feeders in the yard, pool-area runs, and sleeves. Schedule 40 is the standard wall; Schedule 80 is the heavier wall used where the run is exposed to physical damage. PVC may not be used where ambient or conductor heat will exceed its temperature rating, in the hazardous and theater-type locations its article bars, or as a support for fixtures and equipment hanging off it. Underground cover for PVC is 18 in in the general Table 300.5 case. Two field behaviors define the method: it expands and contracts a lot with temperature, and its joints are solvent-welded, not threaded (except at listed threaded fittings and adapters). PVC is nonmetallic, so the raceway itself is never the ground path — an equipment grounding conductor goes in the run where one is required.

The support numbers (Table 352.30) — PVC is supported far more often than metal raceway, because it sags:
• 1/2 in through 1 in — every 3 ft
• 1-1/4 in through 2 in — every 5 ft
• 2-1/2 in through 3 in — every 6 ft
• 3-1/2 in through 5 in — every 7 ft
• 6 in — every 8 ft
And the expansion numbers (Table 352.44): a 100 ft run of PVC changes length about 2 in with a 50°F temperature swing, and about 4.1 in with a 100°F swing. An expansion fitting is required where the expected change in length reaches 1/4 in — a threshold a short exposed Florida riser can cross between a winter morning and a summer afternoon.
sections.on_the_job: Expansion is the inspection item apprentices forget: a long straight run in Florida sun moves. Where the expected length change reaches 1/4 in, an expansion fitting belongs in the run — the exact trigger and the movement math are flagged for Mike's check in the companion lookup, and the support spacings come from this article's support table, not from habit.
sections.figure_idea: Long PVC run down a block wall with an expansion fitting mid-run, sun arrows on the wall, and a support strap spacing callout.
sections.florida_note: Florida sun on an exposed PVC riser is the textbook expansion case — check every long south- and west-wall run.

sections.title: Supporting PVC — the Table 352.30 intervals
sections.plain_explanation:
PVC is secured within 3 ft of each box, cabinet, or termination, and supported at the intervals of Table 352.30, which grow with the conduit size:
• 1/2 in through 1 in — every 3 ft
• 1-1/4 in through 2 in — every 5 ft
• 2-1/2 in through 3 in — every 6 ft
• 3-1/2 in through 5 in — every 7 ft
• 6 in — every 8 ft
The table assumes the conduit is supported so it cannot sag between straps; a run that bellies between supports will belly worse once the Florida sun and the conductors are in it.
sections.on_the_job: On a 1 in yard run, a strap every 3 ft feels like a lot — until you see the same run in August with two straps missing. Strap to the table at rough-in; adding straps after the trench is closed means hand-digging your own work.
sections.figure_idea: PVC run along a wall with support intervals dimensioned for 1 in (3 ft) and 2 in (5 ft), and straps marked within 3 ft of the panel.

sections.title: Expansion fittings — PVC moves
sections.plain_explanation: PVC grows and shrinks with temperature far more than the building it is attached to — roughly 4 in of length change per 100 ft of run for a 100°F temperature swing (Table 352.44 gives the exact characteristic). Where the expected length change is 1/4 in or more, a listed expansion fitting is required, so the movement happens at the fitting instead of pulling couplings apart, pushing into boxes, or bowing the run off the wall. Underground runs meet the same rule where they rise out of the ground into the sun.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: a 40 ft PVC run on a sunny Florida wall, installed at 70°F, with surface temperatures reaching 150°F — an 80°F swing. Movement is about 40 ft × (4 in per 100 ft) × 0.8, roughly 1.3 in. That is five times the 1/4 in threshold: the run gets an expansion fitting, set at mid-travel for the installation temperature.
sections.figure_idea: Long PVC wall run with an expansion fitting at mid-run, arrows showing the piston travel, and a thermometer scale from installation temperature to summer peak.
sections.florida_note: Florida is expansion-fitting country: attic, roof, and sunlit-wall temperatures swing far past the indoor range, and a long PVC run glued rigid at both ends will find the weakest coupling by the second summer.

sections.title: High-density polyethylene conduit — Type HDPE
sections.plain_explanation: HDPE conduit is the coiled, flexible nonmetallic raceway used mainly for long underground runs — directional-bored and trenched duct for utilities, site feeders and communications — joined by fusion or listed couplings rather than solvent cement. Its strength is the continuous long run with no joints in the bore.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma meets HDPE most often as the duct the utility or site contractor provides. Confirm what is actually in the duct and who owns it before planning a pull through it.

sections.title: Nonmetallic underground conduit with conductors — Type NUCC
sections.plain_explanation: NUCC is a factory assembly: conductors already installed inside a nonmetallic underground conduit, supplied and installed as one listed system for direct burial work. Because it arrives as a system, its fittings, splices and repairs follow its own article and listing — it is not field-pulled PVC with a head start.
sections.on_the_job: Rare on Sharma work. Treat any NUCC found underground as a system to be identified before it is cut or extended.

sections.title: Reinforced thermosetting resin conduit — Type RTRC
sections.plain_explanation: RTRC is a fiberglass-reinforced resin raceway chosen where corrosion resistance and strength matter and metal raceways would rot or are barred — chemical, wastewater and harsh outdoor industrial environments. It is joined with its own fittings and adhesives and supported under its own article. Its baseline support table, Table 355.30, carries the same spacings as PVC's Table 352.30 — 3 ft for trade sizes 1/2 through 1, rising to 8 ft for trade size 6 — and conduit listed for support at a different spacing is permitted to be installed in accordance with that listing.
sections.on_the_job: Specialized work only. If a corrosive-environment job specifies RTRC, its support table and joining instructions come with the material — get them before the run is laid out.

sections.title: Liquidtight flexible nonmetallic conduit — LFNC
sections.plain_explanation:
LFNC is the all-plastic liquidtight flexible raceway — no metal core — used for short flexible connections in wet and outdoor locations where a nonmetallic method is wanted, including many pool and equipment connections. It comes in listed types with different fittings and limits, has a maximum supported length pattern similar to other flex methods, and may not be used where subject to physical damage or beyond its temperature and listing limits.

The working numbers (356.30): LFNC is fastened within 12 in of each termination and supported at intervals not over 3 ft, with the familiar flex exceptions — fished lengths, short lengths at terminals where flexibility is needed, and up to 6 ft at a luminaire or equipment connection in an accessible ceiling. The tubing itself is plastic and carries nothing: where LFNC is the raceway for a circuit, the equipment grounding conductor runs inside it like any other nonmetallic method.
sections.on_the_job: On pool and outdoor equipment, confirm the specific LFNC type and its fittings are listed for the location before it goes on the truck — 'liquidtight' on the box is a listing claim, not a description.

sections.title: Electrical metallic tubing — EMT
sections.plain_explanation: EMT is the thin-wall steel raceway that carries most of Sharma's light-commercial work: unthreaded, joined with set-screw or compression couplings and connectors, bent on the job with a hand or mechanical bender. It may be used exposed or concealed, in dry, damp and wet locations — in wet locations with fittings that comply with 314.15 and with supports, straps, bolts and screws of corrosion-resistant material or protected against corrosion. Galvanized steel and stainless steel EMT may be installed in concrete, in direct contact with the earth, and in areas subject to severe corrosive influences where protected by corrosion protection and approved as suitable for the condition; aluminum EMT encased in concrete or in direct contact with the earth must have approved supplementary corrosion protection. In cinder concrete or cinder fill subject to permanent moisture, galvanized or stainless EMT is allowed only when protected on all sides by at least 2 in. of noncinder concrete or installed at least 18 in. under the fill. EMT serves as its own equipment grounding conductor when installed with listed fittings made up properly. It may not be used where subject to severe physical damage, to support luminaires or other equipment — except a conduit body no larger than the largest trade size of the tubing — or threaded in the field like rigid conduit: EMT is not threaded, except for factory-threaded integral couplings.
sections.on_the_job: EMT is a system, not a tube: tube + listed fittings + tight make-up = the raceway and the ground path in one. A loose set-screw coupling is a loose ground.
sections.sharma_note: S-01 on commercial EMT work: 20A minimum branch circuits, 12 AWG copper minimum.
sections.figure_idea: EMT run across a commercial ceiling with a bend, a compression coupling and a support strap, each tagged.

sections.title: Where EMT may — and may not — be used
sections.plain_explanation: EMT's permitted list covers most of a commercial building: exposed or concealed, in wet locations where the fittings are listed for wet use (raintight), embedded in concrete, and in masonry in contact with the earth where protected against corrosion. EMT is itself steel, and it is permitted as the equipment grounding path (250.118(4)) — which is why its couplings must be made up tight. The not-permitted list is short: EMT may not be used where it will be subject to severe physical damage during installation or afterward, and it is never threaded in the field — EMT is joined with threadless fittings only.
sections.on_the_job: Two field checks: a wet location means raintight-listed fittings, not standard compression fittings and a prayer; and every coupling wrench-tight, because on an EMT job the raceway is the ground path — a loose set-screw is a loose ground.
sections.figure_idea: EMT run at a wet exterior wall with raintight fittings tagged, and a hand-cut thread on a piece of EMT crossed out.

sections.title: How many conductors fit in EMT — the Chapter 9 handoff
sections.plain_explanation: This section does not carry its own fill numbers: the number of conductors in EMT is whatever Chapter 9 allows — Table 1 percentages (53% for one conductor, 31% for two, 40% for more than two, 60% for a nipple 24 in or shorter), Table 4 areas for the raceway, and Table 5 areas for the conductors. Worked example from the v1 Chapter 9 tables: 1/2 in EMT has a 40% area of 0.122 sq in; a 12 AWG THHN conductor occupies 0.0133 sq in; 0.122 / 0.0133 = 9.17, so nine 12 AWG THHN fit. Equipment grounds count toward fill.
sections.on_the_job: Do the area math, do not eyeball a stuffed pipe at trim time. When all conductors are the same size, Annex C gives the same answer as a shortcut — but the tables are the rule, Annex C is the shortcut.
sections.figure_idea: Calculation card: 0.122 ÷ 0.0133 = 9.17 → 9 conductors, with a 1/2 in EMT cross-section holding nine dots.

sections.title: EMT bends — radius and the 360-degree rule
sections.plain_explanation: Bends in EMT have to be made so the tubing is not damaged and its inside diameter is not effectively reduced. The radius of the curve of any field bend, measured to the centerline of the tubing, must not be less than the radius shown in Chapter 9, Table 2 for that trade size. Offsets and saddles count toward the run's total bend. Between pull points, the total bend in one run may not exceed 360 degrees: the equivalent of four quarter bends, in any combination. A run that needs more than 360 degrees needs a pull point — a box or conduit body — not a stronger pull.
sections.on_the_job: Count every bend on your fingers as you lay out: stub-up 90, offset 30 + 30, three-point saddle 22.5 + 45 + 22.5 — you are at 240 before the run leaves the room. Plan the pull points while the ceiling is open.
sections.figure_idea: Run diagram with bend angles added in a running total: 90 + 30 + 30 + 45 = 195°, marked 'under 360 — OK'.

sections.title: Securing and supporting EMT
sections.plain_explanation: EMT must be securely fastened within 3 ft of each outlet box, junction box, device box, cabinet, conduit body or other tubing termination, and securely fastened and supported at intervals not exceeding 10 ft. Where structural members do not readily permit fastening within 3 ft of a termination, an unbroken length of EMT — a length without couplings — may be fastened up to 5 ft from that termination. For concealed work in finished buildings or prefinished wall panels where securing is impracticable, unbroken lengths without a coupling may be fished. Horizontal runs supported by openings through framing members at intervals not exceeding 10 ft, and securely fastened within 3 ft of a termination, are permitted to count as supported by that framing.
sections.on_the_job: Strap rhythm in the field: strap at 3 ft from the box, then every 10 ft, and a strap on each side of a coupling run that wants to sag. If the tube moves when you pull wire, it was not supported.
sections.figure_idea: Ceiling run with straps dimensioned: 3 ft max from the box, 10 ft max between straps.

sections.title: EMT couplings and connectors — tight, and listed for the location
sections.plain_explanation: EMT couplings and connectors must be made up tight so the raceway is mechanically continuous and electrically continuous as a ground path. Where buried in masonry or concrete, they must be of the concrete-tight type. Where installed in wet locations, they must comply with 314.15 — listed for use in wet locations and installed so moisture does not enter or accumulate in the enclosure. The Code rule is the listing for the location, not the fitting style: use the type, compression or set-screw, that is listed concrete-tight or listed for wet use for the job in front of you.
sections.on_the_job: Match the fitting to the location on the purchase order, not at the truck: a fitting listed concrete-tight for masonry or concrete, a fitting listed for wet use for wet locations, and ordinary fittings only where the run stays dry and is not buried in masonry or concrete.
sections.figure_idea: Two fittings side by side: set-screw marked 'dry', compression marked 'wet / concrete-tight'.

sections.title: Flexible metallic tubing — Type FMT
sections.plain_explanation: FMT is a small, flexible metallic tubing method for specific limited applications — not a general raceway and not the same thing as FMC (Article 348), despite the similar name and look. Its permitted uses are narrow and its size range is small.
sections.on_the_job: Name-check before use: FMT on a print is a specific listed method. Do not substitute FMC, EMT or LFMC for it by appearance.

sections.title: Electrical nonmetallic tubing — ENT ('smurf tube')
sections.plain_explanation: ENT is a pliable, corrugated nonmetallic raceway used concealed in walls, floors and ceilings, in slab on grade and in other locations its article allows — common on Sharma-adjacent work for low-voltage and island/concrete runs in houses, and as a sleeve where a future pull is wanted. It is not a general substitute for PVC conduit: its locations, support rules (commonly every 3 ft and within 3 ft of boxes, per its article) and temperature and damage limits are its own.
sections.on_the_job: Island receptacle in a slab house is the classic ENT case: stub it accurately, cap it, photograph it with measurements before the pour — a lost stub in concrete is a saw-cut later.
sections.figure_idea: Slab section with a corrugated ENT run to a kitchen island stub-up, tape measure to two walls in the photo callout.

sections.title: Where ENT may — and may not — be used
sections.plain_explanation: ENT ('smurf tube') is permitted concealed in walls, floors, and ceilings, encased in concrete and in slab-on-grade work with listed fittings, and in wet locations where the tubing and fittings are listed for them. Its exposed use is height-limited: exposed ENT is permitted only in buildings not more than three floors above grade (with this section's own allowances), which is why it disappears into slabs and walls on taller work. It may not be used where subject to physical damage, in sunlight unless marked sunlight resistant, in hazardous (classified) locations except as specifically allowed, for circuits over 600 volts, or as a support for fixtures or other equipment.
sections.on_the_job: In a Florida slab, ENT is a sleeve and low-voltage raceway more than a branch-circuit method: coil and stub it where the island and floor outlets will land, cap the ends against concrete, and photograph every run before the pour — after the pour, the photo is the as-built.
sections.figure_idea: Slab plan with ENT coils stubbed at an island and a floor outlet, caps on the ends, and a camera icon marking the pre-pour photo.

sections.title: Auxiliary gutters
sections.plain_explanation: An auxiliary gutter is a sheet-metal enclosure hung at switchboards, panelboards and service equipment to give conductors room to enter, turn and distribute where the equipment's own wiring space runs out. It supplements the equipment — it is not a raceway run across a building, and its conductor fill and splicing room follow its own article.
sections.on_the_job: On larger services and multi-meter work, a gutter is what makes a clean, legal lineup possible. Size it for the conductors and their bending, like 312.6, before the gear is set.

sections.title: Busways
sections.plain_explanation: A busway is a factory-built distribution system: busbars in a metal housing, with plug-in units that tap power off along the run — the backbone distribution of larger commercial and industrial buildings. Sections are joined, supported and tapped as a listed system; overcurrent protection and grounding follow its article and the system design.
sections.on_the_job: Outside Sharma's ordinary scope, but common in the larger commercial spaces Sharma works in. Never open, move or tap a busway as if it were a big wireway — it is energized distribution equipment.

sections.title: Cablebus
sections.plain_explanation: Cablebus is an engineered power-distribution assembly: insulated conductors supported in a ventilated metal enclosure, built to a specific design for large feeders, typically between major equipment. It is designed and supplied as a system for that job, not assembled from shelf parts in the field.
sections.on_the_job: Industrial and large-commercial work only. Field changes to a cablebus run are engineering changes, not electrician improvisation.

sections.title: Cellular concrete floor raceways
sections.plain_explanation: This article covers raceways formed in cellular concrete floor systems in larger commercial buildings, where the floor structure itself contains the distribution cells and header ducts. Outlets are activated from the cells with system fittings.
sections.on_the_job: Encountered in existing commercial buildings, not new Sharma construction. Identifying the floor system correctly is the whole job before any outlet work.

sections.title: Cellular metal floor raceways
sections.plain_explanation: The metal counterpart to Article 372: raceways formed by the cells of a cellular steel floor deck in commercial construction, with header ducts and system outlet fittings. Bonding and continuity of the metal system are part of its article.
sections.on_the_job: Existing-building work. As with 372, the system has to be identified before it is extended or abandoned in place.

sections.title: Metal wireways
sections.plain_explanation: A wireway is a sheet-metal trough with a hinged or removable cover, used in light commercial work to carry feeders and branch circuits where conductors need to be laid in and remain accessible along a run — above panels, along shop walls, in electrical rooms. Conductors are limited by fill and by the number of current-carrying conductors before adjustment applies, splices and taps are allowed inside where the wireway stays accessible, and the cover is what makes the system legal: no cover, no wireway.
sections.on_the_job: Wireway is the tidy alternative to a forest of parallel conduits leaving a panel — plan its size for the conductors plus their derating, not just their bulk.
sections.figure_idea: Electrical room wall: panel with a wireway trough above it, conduits dropping out of the bottom of the trough.

sections.title: Wireway fill — 20 percent, and splices inside
sections.plain_explanation: A wireway is not a trough to fill to the brim. The conductors at any cross section may not exceed 20 percent of the wireway's interior cross-sectional area. Two allowances make wireways practical anyway: the ampacity adjustment (bundling derating) factors do not apply where the number of current-carrying conductors in the wireway is 30 or fewer, and splices and taps are permitted inside a wireway that remains accessible — provided the splices and taps do not fill more than 75 percent of the wiring space at that cross section.
sections.on_the_job: Do the 20 percent math at layout, not with the cover in your hand: list the conductors, take their areas from Chapter 9 Table 5, and check the total against one-fifth of the wireway's inside area. If the count of current-carrying conductors passes 30, derating enters the job — that is the moment to upsize the wireway or split the run.
sections.figure_idea: Wireway cross-section shaded to 20 percent conductor fill, with a splice bay shaded to its 75 percent limit.

sections.title: Nonmetallic wireways
sections.plain_explanation: The nonmetallic counterpart to Article 376's metal wireways: a trough with a removable cover for laying in conductors, used where a nonmetallic system is wanted, within the locations and limits its article sets. Fill, splices and support follow the same wireway logic in a plastic system.
sections.on_the_job: Use where corrosion makes metal wireway a poor choice and the location is permitted. The cover still makes the system — no cover, no wireway.

sections.title: Multioutlet assemblies
sections.plain_explanation: A multioutlet assembly is a surface, flush or freestanding raceway designed to hold conductors and receptacles, assembled at the factory or in the field — the hard-wired strip over a workbench or lab counter, in metal or nonmetallic form. It is permitted in dry locations only. It may not be installed concealed — except that a metal assembly may be surrounded on its back and sides by the building finish and a nonmetallic one may be recessed in a baseboard — and it is barred where subject to severe physical damage, in hoistways, and in the other locations its article lists. A metal assembly may pass through a dry partition if no outlet sits inside the partition and the cover can be removed on both sides. In a dwelling it is not a dodge around the receptacle rules, but it is not banned from counting either: for kitchen countertop spacing, each 12 in of assembly containing two or more receptacles counts as one receptacle outlet under 210.52(C).
sections.on_the_job: Use it where it belongs — benches, counters, retail and lab work — and count its load like any receptacle run; the strip does not create capacity, it only distributes outlets.

sections.title: Nonmetallic extensions
sections.plain_explanation: Nonmetallic extensions are listed surface extension wiring systems that start from an existing outlet to serve additional outlets along a wall surface — a narrow, specific method with its own fittings and limits, not a license to surface-run ordinary cable. They are barred in many of the places people first think of using them.
sections.on_the_job: Rarely the right answer on Sharma work; a proper raceway (386/388) or a new circuit is usually both legal and better. Know the article mainly to recognize the method.

sections.title: Strut-type channel raceway
sections.plain_explanation: A strut-type channel raceway is a listed wiring system built on metal strut channel with covers and fittings made for electrical use — the channel is the raceway. Ordinary structural strut by itself is a support, not a raceway; the listed covers, fittings and conductor limits of this article are what turn it into one.
sections.on_the_job: Common confusion on commercial jobs: strut holding conduits is support work; strut carrying conductors inside it is this article. Keep the two apart in the takeoff and the inspection conversation.

sections.title: Surface metal raceways
sections.plain_explanation: Surface metal raceway is the low-profile metal channel system mounted on walls and ceilings in finished spaces — the office and retail retrofit standard — carrying branch circuits to surface boxes and devices made for the system. Fill, fittings and grounding are the system's own; it is a raceway, not a decorative cover for loose cable.
sections.on_the_job: The retrofit answer where walls cannot open. Plan device boxes and fittings from the same system — mixing ordinary boxes defeats the listing.

sections.title: Surface nonmetallic raceways
sections.plain_explanation: The nonmetallic counterpart to Article 386: surface-mounted plastic raceway systems for finished spaces, common for both power and low-voltage in offices and homes. Power and communications sharing one system is allowed only where the system is listed and arranged for it.
sections.on_the_job: Neat retrofit work, within its damage and location limits — it is surface wiring, so it lives where people and furniture can reach it. Protect or re-route accordingly.

sections.title: Underfloor raceways
sections.plain_explanation: Underfloor raceways are distribution ducts set in or under a concrete floor — the older office-building system of floor ducts and junction boxes feeding floor outlets. New work is uncommon; existing systems are met on commercial remodels, where inserts and outlets must match the system.
sections.on_the_job: On a remodel, find the junction boxes before promising floor outlets. An abandoned duct with no access is archaeology, not distribution.

sections.title: Cable tray systems
sections.plain_explanation: Cable tray is a support system, not a raceway: an open ladder, ventilated or solid-bottom structure that supports the wiring methods listed in Table 392.10(A) — including tray-rated Type TC, metal-clad cable, raceways, and, where identified for the use, nonmetallic-sheathed cable in the structures Article 334 permits. Single insulated conductors are the restricted case: outside the industrial-establishment rules of 392.10(B) they do not belong in tray. The tray itself must be bonded and grounded as the article requires, and fill is figured by the cable-area and sum-of-diameters rules of 392.22, not by the Chapter 9 conduit tables.
sections.on_the_job: If Sharma reaches for tray on a light-commercial job, the cable choice changes first (a wiring method Table 392.10(A) permits for that building), then the tray size. Do not lay loose single building conductors in tray and call it supported — apart from the narrow industrial exception in 392.10(B), they are not a tray wiring method. NM is not automatically barred either: it may sit in tray only where Article 334 permits it and the cable is identified for tray use.
sections.figure_idea: Warehouse bay with a ladder tray carrying bundled tray cable above a conduit drop to a disconnect.

sections.title: Low-voltage suspended ceiling power distribution systems
sections.plain_explanation: This article covers listed low-voltage power systems that use the suspended ceiling structure to distribute power to ceiling-supported equipment — a specific engineered system, not permission to treat ceiling grid as a raceway or support. Components, connections and loads are the system's own.
sections.on_the_job: Specialized commercial systems only. Ordinary ceiling work stays under 300.11 and 300.22 — this article does not loosen either.

sections.title: Concealed knob-and-tube wiring
sections.plain_explanation:
Knob-and-tube is the oldest method in the chapter: single conductors run open on porcelain knobs and through porcelain tubes, found in older Florida houses. This article governs its (very limited) permitted extensions and uses today; new knob-and-tube installations are effectively a closed door, and insulation contact with it is a known fire concern that other codes also address.

The prohibition that matters most on Florida re-insulation jobs sits in 394.12: knob-and-tube is not permitted in the hollow spaces of walls, ceilings, and attics where loose, rolled, or foamed-in-place insulation envelops the conductors. Blowing insulation over live knob-and-tube buries a heat source the method was never designed for, and hides it. Where insulation work is planned over knob-and-tube, the wiring is replaced or the insulation plan changes — that conversation happens before the insulation truck, not after.
sections.on_the_job: On remodels in older houses, Sharma practice is identification and safe handling: document it, do not bury it in new insulation or extend it casually, and put replacement options in front of the customer.
sections.florida_note: Older Florida housing stock — the pre-war bungalows of Tampa, Orlando, and Jacksonville — is where Sharma meets knob-and-tube, and it is exactly where blown-in attic insulation retrofits are sold hardest. Flag it on every survey.

sections.title: Messenger-supported wiring
sections.plain_explanation: Messenger-supported wiring carries cables or conductors on a steel messenger strand strung between structures — overhead spans to outbuildings, site lighting and similar runs, using cable assemblies listed for the method. The messenger carries the load; the electrical cable is not its own support.
sections.on_the_job: Overhead spans live outdoors and age outdoors: check the strand, attachments and clearances as one system at every service call.

sections.title: Open wiring on insulators
sections.plain_explanation: Open wiring on insulators — individual conductors run exposed on insulators with set separations — is a legacy and specialized method (agricultural and industrial settings are its remaining home), governed by its own clearances and protection rules. It is not a shortcut version of knob-and-tube and not a method for new house work.
sections.on_the_job: Know it to recognize it. New Sharma work does not start here.

sections.title: Outdoor overhead conductors over 1,000 volts
sections.plain_explanation: The chapter's last article covers outdoor overhead conductors operating over 1,000 volts on premises wiring — the campus- or plant-style medium-voltage distribution a property owner owns, not the serving utility. It is a short, engineered article, not a clearance table: it sets no prescriptive clearances of its own, 399.30 requires the supporting structures to be designed and documented by a licensed professional engineer, and the detailed clearance and construction rules live in the National Electrical Safety Code. Utility installations under a utility's exclusive control sit outside the NEC altogether under 90.2(B)(5). (Note the number: in the 2020 NEC this article is 399, not 395 — the research draft's body text used 395 before its own index corrected it.)
sections.on_the_job: Not Sharma field work. Its page exists so the book ends where the printed chapter ends, with the right number on it.
